title: New clothes
hookLine: beware of all enterprises that require new clothes (Walden 1)

cards: New running shoes, a new planner, a yoga mat still rolled in plastic. There's a particular hope that lives in a shopping bag: this time it'll be different, because this time there's equipment.
Then the shoes sit by the door. The planner stops in February.

Thoreau saw the same pattern in his own neighbors, with coats and hats instead of sneakers, and in the first chapter of Walden he wrote a warning that sounds almost like a proverb: beware of all enterprises that require new clothes.

teach.b: First, the whole sentence, which has two halves: "I say, beware of all enterprises that require new clothes, and not rather a new wearer of clothes." The second half is the point. The danger isn't clothes.
It's starting with the outside and hoping the inside follows. If something real is changing, he suggests, it changes the person first, and the old coat will do.
Second, the patch on the knee. Thoreau notices how much people fear being seen in old or mended clothes.
Nobody, he says, ever sank in his opinion for wearing a patch, but he suspects plenty of people would rather go into town with a broken leg than with torn trousers. It's a joke, and it isn't.
People often guard their look more carefully than their lives.

Third, fashion as a kind of faith. Each generation, he teases, laughs at old fashions and then follows the new ones with complete devotion, and the tailor is treated almost like an authority on how a person ought to live.
He's not angry. He's amused, and a little sad. Fourth, what this asks of a Tuesday.
Not a vow never to shop again; Thoreau owned clothes and wore them.
Just a small question before any fresh start: does this need new equipment, or a new me?
The run can begin in old shoes. The plan can begin on the back of an envelope. If the change is real, it will still be real in the old coat.

how: Some readers of Walden use 'beware of all enterprises that require new clothes' as a check before a fresh start, beginning with what they already own.

practice: Bring to mind a change you've been meaning to make, and notice if it came with a shopping list attached: gear, an app, a book about the thing instead of the thing. In your mind, set the list down.
What could you do with exactly what you have, wearing what you're wearing right now?
